content: Insulin inhalation is a medication used to manage blood sugar levels in individuals with diabetes. It is prescribed for people with type 1 diabetes, where the body does not produce insulin, and for those with type 2 diabetes who require insulin to control their condition. In type 1 diabetes, it is used alongside long-acting insulin, while in type 2 diabetes, it may be used alone or in combination with other medications. This medication is a short-acting, synthetic form of human insulin that begins to work within 10 to 20 minutes after inhalation and remains effective for approximately 6 hours. It helps regulate blood sugar by facilitating the movement of glucose from the bloodstream into body tissues for energy and by reducing glucose production in the liver. Insulin inhalation is available as a powder that is inhaled through a specially designed inhaler. It is typically taken immediately before meals, within 10 minutes of eating. It is crucial to follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the medication exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency unless instructed by your doctor. Insulin inhalation helps control diabetes but does not cure it, so it is important to continue using it even if you feel well. Do not stop using it or switch to another brand or type of insulin without consulting your doctor. Your doctor may need to adjust the doses of your other diabetes medications, such as long-acting insulin or oral medications, when you start using insulin inhalation. They may also modify your insulin inhalation dose during treatment. Always follow your doctor’s instructions and ask questions if you are unsure about any aspect of your treatment. The powder for insulin inhalation is packaged in small foil dose packets called blisters. Do not open or puncture the blisters; they will open when placed in the inhaler. Do not swallow the contents of the blister or inhale them without the proper inhaler. After using a blister, dispose of it in a trash can that is out of reach of children and pets. Do not attempt to reuse a blister. Avoid substituting three 1-mg blisters for one 3-mg blister, as this may result in an overdose. If necessary, you can use two 1-mg blisters in place of one 3-mg blister, but you should check your blood sugar level and obtain a new supply of 3-mg blisters as soon as possible. Contact your doctor if you develop a cold, cough, or nasal congestion during treatment, as these conditions may require dose adjustments or more frequent blood sugar monitoring. Carefully read the manufacturer’s Medication Guide for instructions on using, cleaning, and maintaining the inhaler. This medication may be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before using insulin inhalation, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to insulin or any of its inactive ingredients. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Certain medications, such as beta blockers, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, and others, may interact with insulin inhalation, requiring dose adjustments or careful monitoring for side effects. Inform your doctor if you smoke, have recently quit smoking, or have a history of lung diseases such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Smoking during treatment is not recommended, and you should stop using insulin inhalation and contact your doctor immediately if you start smoking. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have nerve damage caused by diabetes, kidney or liver disease, or if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while using this medication, notify your doctor. Inform your healthcare provider if you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, or if you experience illness, stress, travel across time zones, or changes in your exercise routine, as these factors may affect your insulin needs. Ask your doctor how often you should check your blood sugar levels and whether you need to test them before driving or operating machinery. Insulin inhalation may reduce lung function, so your doctor will order tests to monitor your lung health before and during treatment. Follow all dietary and exercise recommendations provided by your doctor or dietitian. Maintain a consistent eating schedule with similar amounts and types of food each day. Skipping or delaying meals or altering your diet can disrupt blood sugar control. Alcohol may lower blood sugar levels, so consult your doctor about safe alcohol consumption while using this medication. If you miss a dose, skip it and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Check your blood sugar and contact your doctor if it is too high. This medication may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), such as shakiness, dizziness, sweating, irritability, headache, and blurred vision, and follow your doctor’s instructions for managing these symptoms. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness, requiring immediate medical attention. Similarly, high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) symptoms, such as extreme thirst, frequent urination, and weakness, should be reported to your doctor. Untreated hyperglycemia can result in diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition. Seek medical care immediately if you experience symptoms such as dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid heartbeat, or fruity-smelling breath. Common side effects of insulin inhalation include cough, mild shortness of breath, sore throat, and nasal symptoms. Severe side effects, such as rash, hives, or wheezing, require immediate medical attention. Report any unusual problems to your doctor. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Do not refrigerate or freeze it. Dispose of any medication that is outdated or no longer needed, and consult your pharmacist about proper disposal. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Overdose can cause hypoglycemia, especially if you take too much insulin or eat or exercise less than usual. Follow your doctor’s instructions for managing hypoglycemia if it occurs. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for regular monitoring of your blood sugar and HbA1c levels. Your doctor will also guide you on how to monitor your blood sugar or urine sugar levels at home. Always wear a diabetic identification bracelet to ensure proper treatment in emergencies. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
